ruleIntents.intent: Checks one thing only: does every link element have a non-empty accessible name (computed name != ""). It is a pure name-PRESENCE gate. It does NOT evaluate whether the name is meaningful, descriptive, unique, or conveys the link's destination/purpose — only that some non-empty accessible name string exists. The accessible name can come from any source in the ACCName computation: link text content, aria-label, aria-labelledby, title, or alt on a contained image. An empty/whitespace-only name, a decorative-only image (alt="", role=presentation/none), a broken aria-labelledby reference, or no name at all = fail.
ruleIntents.scLimb: 2.4.4 requires that "the purpose of each link can be determined from the link text alone, or from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context." This rule exercises ONLY the necessary precondition of that — the existence of a non-empty programmatically-determined accessible name (the "link text alone" carrier). It is the floor case (F89-style failure: a link with no accessible name at all). It does NOT test the substantive limb of 2.4.4: whether that name (plus context) actually communicates the link's PURPOSE. A link named "click here" or "more" passes this rule but can still fail 2.4.4. The rule is shared across 2.4.4 / 2.4.9 (AAA) / 4.1.2 (Name) / 1.1.1 (secondary), confirming it tests the name-existence intersection, not link-purpose semantics.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any HTML element that is an "inheriting semantic link" included in the accessibility tree. Concretely: a/area with an href and the (default or inherited) link role; elements with an explicit role="link" (e.g. div, button); elements with a link-inheriting role such as doc-biblioref. The element must be IN the accessibility tree (rendered/exposed). Excluded (inapplicable): elements whose role is overridden to non-link (a role="button"), elements removed from the a11y tree (display:none, visibility:hidden, aria-hidden=true), and elements that never have the link role because they lack href (bare <a>, <area> without href). Note: off-screen/clipped links (position:absolute; left:-9999px) ARE still applicable — they remain in the a11y tree.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope target element has an accessible name that is not the empty string "". Pass = a non-empty computed accessible name exists via any ACCName source. Fail = the computed accessible name is "" (empty or whitespace-only): empty link content, image children that contribute nothing (alt="", role=presentation, role=none, title="", aria-labelledby pointing to empty or non-existent id), or no name source at all. Whitespace-only content (Failed Example 10: role="none" link that stays a link via Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution, content is just a space) is treated as empty.

The name CONTENT is always either the ideal full label ('Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI)') or literally empty — there is no middle ground. Real 2.4.4 failures are dominated by present-but-useless names ('click here', 'read more', 'link', 'here', a bare URL, '>>', an icon-font glyph) which all PASS this rule. The fixtures cannot exercise the SC's actual purpose test.

All passing names are identical/W3C-branded; no test of duplicated link text for different destinations (multiple 'Read more' links), which is a classic real 2.4.4 problem this rule structurally cannot catch.

Image-based links use one stock logo (w3c-logo.png) or a planets imagemap; no real-world icon buttons, SVG icons, sprite/background-image links, CSS-pseudo-element content, or font-icon links where name presence is genuinely ambiguous.

aria-labelledby cases are minimal (single id, present-or-missing); no multi-id token lists, self-reference, forward references, ordering, or labelledby that resolves to whitespace/hidden text — the messy ACCName computation that trips real checkers.

Off-screen handling is tested only via the canonical left:-9999px pattern; no clip-path, height:0/overflow:hidden, opacity:0, sr-only utility classes, or transform-based hiding that determine real a11y-tree membership.

Dynamic/SPA reality is absent: no JS-injected links, links whose name is set after load, links revealed on interaction, or framework components (React/Vue) where the rendered name differs from source markup.
No localization/whitespace edge variety beyond a single space: no non-breaking spaces, zero-width characters, name composed only of punctuation, or emoji-only names.

doc-biblioref is the only exotic inheriting role tested; other link-inheriting roles, area-outside-map browser-support divergences, and Presentational-Roles-Conflict edge cases (called out as accessibility-support caveats) are represented by at most one fixture each, understating real-world AT variance.

Pages are tiny static HTML with no CSS framework, no real layout, and no competing content — so checker behavior here cannot reveal false positives/negatives that arise from scale, deep DOM nesting, shadow DOM, or iframes.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks whether each in-scope link's accessible name COMBINED WITH its programmatically-determined link context is sufficient to convey the link's purpose. It is a semantic/judgment check: for every semantic link exposed in the accessibility tree with a non-empty accessible name, it asks "would the name plus the surrounding programmatic context tell a user where this link goes / what it does?" Links pass when name+context is descriptive (e.g. "See the description of this product"), and fail when the name is generic ("More", "Workshop", "Download") AND no programmatically-associated context (enclosing p/sentence, list item, table header, aria-describedby) supplies the missing meaning. Crucially the rule's notion of "context" is restricted to PROGRAMMATICALLY DETERMINED context (same paragraph, enclosing list item, table cell + associated headers, aria-describedby), not merely text that is visually nearby on the page.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.4.4 "Link Purpose (In Context)": the IN-CONTEXT limb specifically — purpose determinable "from the link text alone or from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context." It exercises the "together with programmatically determined link context" half (G53/H77/H78/H79/H81 territory), not the link-text-alone path nor the 2.4.9 (Link Only) stricter AAA path. It does NOT exercise the SC's "except where the purpose would be ambiguous to users in general" exception — the rule explicitly assumes that exception away (Assumption 1).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any inheriting semantic link (e.g. a[href], role="link") for which BOTH: (1) the link is included in the accessibility tree, and (2) the link has a non-empty accessible name. Excluded as inapplicable: elements whose link role is overridden (a[href] with role="button"), links removed from the a11y tree (display:none), and a elements that are not semantic links (no href, so role is generic). Links with an EMPTY accessible name are out of scope here (handled by the related "Link has non-empty accessible name" rule).
ruleIntents.expectation: For each applicable link, the accessible name of the target element together with its programmatically determined link context describes the purpose of the link. Pass = name+context conveys purpose; Fail = it does not. Outcome mapping per ACT: any Failed outcome means the SC is not satisfied; all-Passed or Inapplicable means the SC "needs further testing" (i.e. a pass here is not a full conformance pass for 2.4.4).

syntheticNarrowness: Every page is a 1-2 element fragment with a single link (or a tiny set of sibling links) and no surrounding page chrome, nav, header/footer, or competing content — real pages have dozens of links where 'descriptive in context' depends on a much richer, noisier DOM.

The descriptive/non-descriptive judgment is made trivial and unambiguous by design: pass cases use fully self-explanatory phrasing ('See the description of this product') and fail cases use canonical generic words ('More', 'Download', 'Workshop', 'Go'). Real-world links live in a large grey zone (e.g. 'Read more about pricing', 'Learn more', 'Click here for the 2024 annual report', truncated titles, marketing copy) that these binary extremes never probe.

The 'purpose' is always a same-page anchor (#desc, #main) or a stub external URL; the link target's actual destination/function is never the discriminator — only the literal text is. Real 2.4.4 failures often hinge on text that reads fine but mismatches the destination (e.g. 'Home' linking to a PDF), which is untestable here.

Context-supplying mechanisms are shown one-at-a-time in isolation (one paragraph, one list, one table, one aria-describedby) with the descriptive token placed exactly where the technique prescribes. No case mixes mechanisms, has deeply nested/ambiguous ancestry, multiple candidate paragraphs, or context that is partially helpful — so the boundary of what counts as 'programmatically determined context' is only sampled at clean extremes.

Repeated/adjacent links that share text but differ in destination — the most common real 2.4.4 problem ('Read more' x10 in a card grid, identical 'Edit'/'Delete' across table rows) — are not represented; the table/list pass cases give each link a DIFFERENT name (HTML/EPUB/Plain text) so they sidestep the duplicate-name disambiguation problem entirely.
Language/locale, RTL, screen-reader pronunciation, visually-hidden helper text spans, title-attribute fallbacks, icon-font links, and image-map/area links (H24 is cited but never tested) are absent.
The SC's central 'ambiguous to users in general' exception is explicitly assumed away rather than tested, so the rule/test set never exercises the hardest judgment 2.4.4 actually requires.

Failed cases are constructed so the missing context is OBVIOUSLY just-out-of-reach (text in a sibling p, or outside the ul, or in a non-header cell) to teach the 'programmatic vs visual proximity' distinction; this is pedagogically clean but does not reflect the messy partial-association cases (e.g. CSS-positioned adjacency, aria-owns, table scope/headers attributes) auditors face.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that when a page has two or more links that (a) share the SAME non-empty accessible name AND (b) sit in the SAME programmatically-determined link context, those links resolve to the same resource, to equivalent resources, or are ambiguous-to-everyone. In effect it detects the failure mode where identical-looking links (same name, same context) silently go to DIFFERENT destinations, which leaves an AT user unable to tell the links' purposes apart. It is the contrapositive of SC 2.4.4: rather than asking 'does each link's purpose read clearly from text+context', it asks 'do two links that read identically actually behave identically'.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context): the 'determined from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context' limb, read against the 'except where the purpose would be ambiguous to users in general' exception. It targets the negative case — identical (text + context) pairs that diverge in purpose — and explicitly honors the ambiguous-to-all carve-out (Passed Example 9). It deliberately does NOT cover the 'identical (deep-equal) but not same context' variant, nor disambiguation conveyed only visually/non-semantically (those are pushed to 1.3.1 / 1.1.1 in the Background).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to a SET of two or more HTML or SVG elements where ALL of: they are inheriting semantic link nodes (role=link, whether native a/area/svg-a or explicit role=link); in the same web page/HTML document; included in the accessibility tree; have matching (equal) accessible names that are non-empty; and have the SAME (pointer-identical DOM-node set, not merely deep-equal) programmatically determined link context. The test target is the full group sharing one name+context. Inapplicable when: not a link role; names differ; name empty; one link removed from a11y tree (aria-hidden); or contexts differ (different list items, different display blocks, or equivalent-but-not-same DOM contexts).
ruleIntents.expectation: For each pair of links in a target set, at least one holds: both resolve to the same resource (after instant redirects only); OR both resolve to equivalent resources (same purpose / same relevant info, even with different layout, different file, or instant redirect); OR there is no visual information on the page indicating the links go to non-equivalent resources (i.e. ambiguous to users in general). Failing means two same-name/same-context links go to non-equivalent resources AND something on the page (text differences, adjacent images, CSS background icons, alignment, query params) signals they differ — or a redirect that is non-instant.

The provided passed fixture is the most degenerate case possible (identical href twice), so it exercises only string-equality of URLs, not any of the equivalent-resource or ambiguity judgment that is the rule's actual difficulty.

aspects.title: Generic/boilerplate link text with a non-empty name but no purpose, and no context that rescues it (G91/H30 substantive failure)
aspects.description: A link whose accessible name exists and is non-empty but is generic boilerplate ('click here', 'read more', 'more', 'here', 'details', 'learn more', 'link', 'continue', '>>') or is just the bare URL, AND for which no programmatically determined link context (the same sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell, or associated table-header cell, or aria-label/labelledby/describedby) supplies the missing purpose. The name passes the only APPROVED rule (c487ae) trivially because it is a pure name-presence gate. The judgment is irreducibly semantic: read the link text plus its containing block and decide whether a user can infer the destination's purpose without leaving the link. Includes the bare-URL case, where the Understanding/G91 say the URI is 'generally not sufficiently descriptive'. The borderline case — where context ALMOST but not-quite rescues a generic name — is the hardest and the most valuable.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the substantive limb of 2.4.4: whether the link text, alone or with its programmatically determined link context, actually conveys the link's PURPOSE — not merely that a non-empty name exists (the c487ae floor).
aspects.whyUncovered: The only APPROVED rule (c487ae) is a pure name-PRESENCE gate; 'click here' passes it. The substantive limb lives only in PROPOSED, unapproved rule 5effbb, whose failed examples use stilted single-word names ('More', 'Workshop', 'Go') on otherwise-empty pages, never the real-world boilerplate a person actually meets, and never the borderline case where residual context nearly rescues a generic name. A fully-automated checker can flag a hard-coded blocklist of phrases but cannot decide whether the surrounding prose makes the purpose inferable — that is a meaning judgment a human must make.

references.quote: Whenever possible, provide link text that identifies the purpose of the link without needing additional context.
The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.
Note that simply providing the URI of the destination is generally not sufficiently descriptive.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build single self-contained pages each centered on one or a few links whose accessible name is generic or a bare URL. Vary whether the SAME block (sentence/paragraph/list-item/cell) supplies purpose words: a FAIL has 'Read more' alone in its own paragraph or a footer of three 'Details' links each in its own <li> with no other text; a near-PASS embeds the same generic phrase in a sentence that already names the destination ('For pricing details, click here.'). Include one page whose link's entire accessible text is a raw URL with no other context. Keep markup minimal so c487ae passes everywhere and only the purpose-sufficiency judgment separates pass from fail.
suggestedScenarios: A standalone paragraph reading only 'Read more' (link is the whole paragraph) with no purpose words anywhere in that block — fails.
The sentence 'For pricing details, click here.' where the purpose ('pricing details') precedes the generic phrase in the same sentence — passes via G53.

A footer containing three list items, each just '
  • Details
    • ', with no distinguishing text — names present, purpose absent, fails.
A link whose entire accessible name is the raw URL 'https://example.com/products/2024/q3-report.pdf' with no surrounding context — bare-URI insufficiency, judge must decide it fails.

A glyph link reading '>>' immediately after a product name in the same sentence ('iPhone 15 Pro >>') — context rescues it (pass); contrast a sibling page with the same '>>' alone in a bare paragraph (fail).
A 'Learn more' link placed inside a <figure><figcaption> that describes a chart, where the caption is the link's containing block — borderline pass requiring the judge to read the caption.

aspects.title: Purpose visible on the page but located OUTSIDE the programmatic link context (F63 — wrong container, including context that follows the link)
aspects.description: The information needed to understand a vague link IS present and visible — a sighted reader can find it — but it sits in content that is NOT programmatically associated with the link: a different paragraph, an adjacent (non-header) table cell, a different list item, a layout-table row above, or text that FOLLOWS the link in the same visual region. The page LOOKS fine, which is exactly the trap. The judgment requires reasoning about DOM container boundaries (sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell/associated <th>) AND about reading-order direction: Understanding and G53 warn that context which follows the link is confusing for screen-reader users reading top to bottom. This is distinct from the generic-text aspect: here the purpose words exist but the question is association and ordering, not absence.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the 'programmatically determined link context' clause of 2.4.4: purpose must come from the link text plus context that is directly associated with the link, not from arbitrary nearby text a user would have to leave the link to find.
aspects.whyUncovered:
5effbb has a few canonical F63-flavoured failures (the W3C 'Workshop'-in-a-different-

, Gutenberg-list, and table 'Download' examples), but they are the exact W3C fixtures and all use the same 'context-in-the-wrong-block' shape. The corpus does NOT exercise context that FOLLOWS the link in the same region (the explicit ordering hazard), context split across a layout-table row, dt/dd associations, or visually-adjacent siblings a person would assume are associated. Deciding whether nearby text is in the same sentence/paragraph/cell requires parsing prose-sentence boundaries and judging programmatic association — and the residual-context sufficiency is semantic; an automated tool cannot do this reliably.

references.quote: This describes a failure condition when the context needed for understanding the purpose of a link is located in content that is not programmatically determined link context.
Because the link is not in the same paragraph as the lead sentence, the user cannot easily discover what the link will let the user read more about.
If the description follows the link, there can be confusion and difficulty for screen reader users who are reading through the page in order (top to bottom).
"Programmatically determined link context" is limited to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where the purpose words clearly exist on the page but the link is in a different programmatic container or the words follow the link. Mirror F63's two canonical shapes (adjacent paragraph; adjacent layout-table cell/row) but extend with the uncovered variants: context-follows-the-link ordering, dt/dd, and a data-table cell whose meaning depends on a <td> styled as a header rather than a real <th>. Each page must look visually coherent so that only the association/ordering analysis reveals the failure.
suggestedScenarios:
Two stacked paragraphs: '

The city council approved a new downtown bike-lane network.

Read more

' — purpose in the prior paragraph, not the link's block; fails F63.

Link placed in its OWN paragraph BEFORE the descriptive sentence ('

Read more

about the council's new bike-lane network.

') — context follows in a separate block, the ordering hazard Understanding warns about.
A layout table where row 1 cell = 'Download the 2024 Annual Report' and row 2 cell = '' — describing text is in a different row (F63's audio-player shape).
A data table where 'Download' sits in a cell whose meaning depends on a column label that is a styled <td>, not a <th>, so it is not an associated header.

A definition list '
Quarterly earnings call recording
Listen
' — judge whether dt/dd counts as programmatically determined link context (arguably not in the enumerated list).

A product grid where each card's description is a sibling
of the link
('View') in a different display block — visually associated, programmatically unrelated.

aspects.title: Image/icon/SVG-only links with a non-empty name that misdescribes or fails to convey the rendered glyph's purpose (F89 semantic-mismatch variant)
aspects.description: A link contains only an image, SVG, or icon-font glyph and DOES have a non-empty accessible name (alt, aria-label, title, or aria-labelledby), so F89's empty-name failure and c487ae both PASS — but the name does not match what the glyph depicts or where the link goes. Examples: a magnifying-glass icon labelled 'image' / 'icon1' / the filename 'search.png'; a social brand glyph labelled the generic 'social'; a printer icon whose alt says 'document'; a hamburger menu whose aria-label says 'logo'; an icon-font link whose accessible name is a literal private-use codepoint that conveys nothing; a back-arrow whose alt says 'forward'. The string exists and looks plausible, so it survives every name-presence check, but a person looking at the rendered icon sees the label is wrong or uselessly generic for the link's purpose. Requires VISUAL judgment of the rendered glyph against the name.
aspects.scLimb: Tests whether the accessible name carried by a non-text-only link actually DESCRIBES the link's purpose, beyond the c487ae/F89 floor of merely having some non-empty name.
aspects.whyUncovered: c487ae's image-link cases only test name presence vs absence on a single stock logo or planets imagemap; a 'wrong but present' alt passes every one. 5effbb's icon examples are always correctly-labelled passes or empty-text fails — never a non-empty-but-wrong label. F89 itself only fires on the empty case. Detecting the mismatch requires looking at the rendered icon and comparing it to the accessible name (and destination) — an automated tool has no notion of what a glyph depicts, so this is irreducibly visual/semantic and human-only.

references.quote: This failure condition occurs when a link contains only non-text content, such as an image, and that link cannot be identified by an accessible name.
The text of, or associated with, the link is intended to describe the purpose of the link.
The img has a text alternative which is the name used for the icon in the site help, which describes clicking the home page icon.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with icon-only links that render an unambiguous, recognizable glyph (inline SVG or a simple shape so the visual model can read it) while the accessible name is either generic ('image', 'icon1', 'link', 'social') or actively contradicts the glyph (back-arrow alt='forward', envelope alt='settings'). Keep at least one PASS where the icon's name correctly matches the glyph's purpose, so the discriminator is the glyph-vs-name comparison, not the presence of a name. Ensure each link has a non-empty computed name so c487ae and F89 both pass.
suggestedScenarios: A toolbar of three icon-only links: magnifying glass with alt='img_2031', gear with aria-label='settings.svg', envelope with aria-label='link' — all non-empty, none descriptive of purpose.
A back-pointing arrow link '' where the alt contradicts the rendered direction of the arrow.
A social-media row where every brand glyph link carries the identical generic aria-label 'social media' — names present but indistinguishable in purpose.
An icon-font trash-can glyph link whose accessible name is a literal private-use-area codepoint string (non-empty, conveys nothing).
A card with a download-arrow icon link whose alt is the surrounding article's title ('How to bake bread') instead of 'Download recipe PDF'.
A correctly-labelled control page (home-icon link with alt='Home', printer icon with aria-label='Print this page') as the PASS contrast.

aspects.title: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
aspects.description: Two or more links on the page share the same accessible name AND the same programmatically determined context, yet lead to different resources serving different purposes — the classic 'three Read more / three Download / two Contact us' problem. The judgment is doubly semantic: (a) are the contexts truly identical, and (b) do the destinations serve EQUIVALENT purposes or genuinely different ones? Equivalent (e.g. the same data offered as PDF/XLSX/CSV) can PASS; genuinely different destinations (chat page vs phone page; sales@ vs support@) FAIL. On a self-contained page this is testable using same-page #fragment anchors and mailto:/tel: targets whose differing purposes are determinable from the page. The disambiguation can also be visual-only (alignment with an image or price block above), which a tool cannot read.
aspects.scLimb: Reflects the 2.4.4 best-practice that links with different purposes have different text; when names AND context are identical but purposes differ, at least one link fails to let the user determine its purpose.
aspects.whyUncovered: fd3a94 is PROPOSED/unapproved and explicitly notFullyAutomatable; its examples are fixed W3C 'About us / Contact us' pairs that require fetching external W3C test-asset URLs to resolve, so they are unusable as self-contained single-page fixtures and never cover same-page #fragments or mailto/tel disambiguation. No APPROVED corpus test exercises duplicate-name disambiguation at all. Resolving 'equivalent purpose' is irreducibly a meaning judgment, and visual-only disambiguation cannot be read by an automated tool.

references.quote: It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.
if two or more links have the same accessible name but resolve to different resources, at least one of them does not accurately describe its purpose.

These two HTML a elements have the same accessible name and context, but go to different resources. Their purpose is disambiguated for sighted users by the alignment of the links with the images above.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build single self-contained pages with two-or-more same-named, same-context links whose differing purposes are resolvable WITHOUT leaving the page — use same-page #fragment anchors that target genuinely different on-page sections, or mailto:/tel: targets whose purpose differs. Include a PASS case where same-named links go to equivalent resources (same data, different format). For the visual-only case, render two identical 'Buy now' links under price blocks so only the layout disambiguates. Keep contexts genuinely identical so the discriminator is purpose-equivalence, not context difference.
suggestedScenarios: Two same-context inline links both named 'order form', one href='#cake-form' and one href='#bread-form' (same-page anchors to genuinely different sections) — different purpose, identical name/context, fails.

Three 'Download' links in one sentence pointing to budget.pdf, budget.xlsx, budget.csv (same data, different format) — equivalent purpose, passes; contrast a sibling page with three 'Download' links to three different documents, fails.
Two 'Email us' links in the same paragraph, one mailto:sales@ and one mailto:support@ — different purposes, identical names, no disambiguating context, fails.
A two-column pricing layout with 'Buy now' under a $9 plan and 'Buy now' under a $99 plan, the price in a sibling block above (visual-only disambiguation) — names and immediate context identical.
Two icon links both aria-label='Map' in the same cell, one to a Google Maps URL and one to an in-page interactive map anchor — judge whether the purposes are equivalent.
Two 'Contact us' links in the same paragraph that both jump to the same '#contact' section (truly equivalent) — passes, as the negative control.

aspects.title: Sufficiency of preceding-heading / list-grouping context as the purpose carrier (H80 judgment, including when the heading is NOT the link's context)
aspects.description: A vague link ('Map', 'Book now', 'PDF', 'Read more') is rescued — or not — by a preceding heading or by the grouping structure it sits in (a section heading above a nav of links, a hotel-block heading, a document offered in three formats under one heading, a card whose <h2> headline is the appended 'Read more' link's group). The H80 judgment is whether the link text combined with that preceding heading describes the purpose, AND whether the heading is genuinely the link's context versus merely visually-above content. This is distinct from F63 (which is about context in the WRONG container) and from generic-text-alone: here the heading/grouping mechanism is the intended carrier, and the call is whether it sufficiently and correctly associates. Repeated identical link sets under different headings ('Map'/'Photos'/'Book now' for two hotels) are the canonical case where context is the only differentiator.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the 'link text together with its programmatically determined link context' clause where the carrier is a preceding heading or grouping structure — whether that combination conveys purpose and whether the heading is actually the link's context.
aspects.whyUncovered: H80 is an advisory technique with no ACT rule of its own; the approved c487ae corpus ignores context entirely, and 5effbb's context cases do not exercise preceding-heading or grouped-nav sufficiency, nor the repeated-link-set-under-different-headings pattern where the heading is the sole differentiator. Judging whether 'Map' under a hotel heading conveys 'map of THIS hotel' — and whether the heading is the link's actual context rather than coincidentally-above text — requires reading the heading and the grouping and making a meaning call no automated checker can make.

references.quote: The preceding heading provides context for an otherwise unclear link. The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.

This can be achieved by putting the description of the link in the same sentence, paragraph, list item, or table cell as the link, or in the table header cell for a link in a data table, because these are directly associated with the link itself.
This context will be most usable if it precedes the link.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages mirroring H80's three example shapes (hotel blocks with repeated nav links under per-hotel headings; one document offered as HTML/PDF/RTF under a single heading; a news card whose <h2> headline groups an appended 'Read more'). Create PASS variants where the preceding heading clearly supplies purpose and is associated (e.g. nav aria-labelledby the heading), and FAIL variants where the heading is visually above but in a different grouping so it is not the link's context, or where even with the heading the combination is still ambiguous. Keep all names non-empty so c487ae passes.
suggestedScenarios: Two hotel blocks, each an <h2> name followed by a list of identical link labels ('Map', 'Photos', 'Book now'); in the PASS the list <nav> is aria-labelledby the hotel heading; in the FAIL the headings sit above unrelated grouping so 'Map' cannot be tied to a specific hotel.

A single

Annual Report 2006-2007

followed by three links 'HTML' 'PDF' 'RTF' — heading supplies purpose, passes (H80 example 2).

A news card: '

Stock market soars

...excerpt...

Read more

' where the 'Read more' shares the card grouping with the headline — judge whether the grouping makes purpose determinable.
Two 'Read more' links each in its own card, the only differentiator being each card's <h2> headline two blocks up — context-as-sole-differentiator case.
A page where a heading 'Downloads' is followed by a 'PDF' link, but a second 'PDF' link lower on the page falls under no heading at all — same name, one rescued by heading context and one not.

A nav of 'Edit' links where each is preceded by an <h3> naming a different record ('Invoice 1042', 'Invoice 1043') — judge whether the preceding heading sufficiently distinguishes the otherwise-identical 'Edit' links.

aspects.title: A specific, well-formed link name that contradicts its actual on-page destination (deceptive but descriptive name)
aspects.description: The link has a clear, descriptive, non-empty accessible name that reads as 'good' in isolation, but it is WRONG about where the link goes. On a self-contained page this is testable when the destination is a same-page #fragment anchor (or a labelled on-page section) whose actual content is verifiable: a 'Read our Privacy Policy' link whose href is '#terms' (a Terms section that exists on the page); a 'Skip to main content' link pointing to '#footer' instead of '#main'; a table-of-contents entry 'Chapter 3: Results' whose anchor actually holds Chapter 5; a 'Basic — $0/mo : Get started' link jumping to an '#enterprise-checkout' section. The name passes every presence and descriptiveness heuristic; the failure is that the name does not describe the link's ACTUAL purpose. This is the inverse of generic text — the text is specific but false — and requires a human to cross-check the claimed purpose against the on-page target.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the core intent of 2.4.4 — that the link's name lets the user understand its purpose and decide whether to follow it — by exposing names that misrepresent the actual (on-page-verifiable) destination.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT fixture (approved and proposed) assumes the name honestly reflects the destination; 5effbb's whole premise is 'does the name describe the purpose' under the implicit assumption the author is not lying. There is NO test where a high-quality descriptive name points to a contradictory target. An automated tool would have to semantically understand the destination and compare it to the link text's claim — a meaning-level cross-check only a human can perform, here scoped to same-page anchors so the destination is verifiable on the single page.

references.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to help users understand the purpose of each link so they can decide whether they want to follow the link.
Having the link and the title agree, or be very similar, is good practice and provides continuity between the link 'clicked on' and the web page that the user lands on.
if two or more links have the same accessible name but resolve to different resources, at least one of them does not accurately describe its purpose.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build single self-contained pages with several labelled on-page sections reachable by #fragment anchors, then point a descriptively-named link at the WRONG section that nonetheless exists on the page, so the judge can open the target and verify the contradiction without leaving the page. Include a PASS control where the descriptive name matches the correct anchor. Keep every name specific and high-quality so the only failure is name-vs-destination mismatch, not name quality.
suggestedScenarios: A page with '#privacy' (a Privacy Policy section) and '#terms' (a Terms of Service section); a link reading 'Read our Privacy Policy' whose href is '#terms' — name describes the wrong on-page section.
A 'Skip to main content' link whose href points to '#footer' instead of the existing '#main' landmark.
A table-of-contents entry 'Chapter 3: Results' whose anchor scrolls to the on-page block that actually holds Chapter 5.
A pricing table whose 'Basic — $0/mo : Get started' link href jumps to an on-page '#enterprise-checkout' section describing the paid tier.
A 'Download the free 2024 calendar' link whose href is an on-page '#newsletter-signup' form section.
A correctly-wired control: 'Read our Privacy Policy' link whose href is '#privacy' and that section is the Privacy Policy — the PASS contrast.

pages.scenario: Local-newspaper front page: a lead story ends with a paragraph whose entire content is a single link reading 'Read more'. The only descriptive text (the headline) is in a different block (the <h2>), which is not programmatically determined link context.
pages.mechanism:
The link's programmatically determined context is its own

, which contains only the generic phrase 'Read more' with no purpose words; the descriptive headline sits in a separate block and is not same-sentence/paragraph/list-item/cell nor aria-linked, so a screen-reader user on the Links List hears only 'Read more, link' and cannot determine the destination (the F63 adjacent-block condition).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <a> has a non-empty computable accessible name ('Read more') confirmed via the Chrome AX tree, so axe link-name, WAVE, Lighthouse, and ACT c487ae all pass; there is only one such link so identical-text heuristics never fire. Deciding that the link's OWN block supplies no purpose, and that the headline in a separate block does not count as programmatic context, is an irreducible human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: A news service lists the first few sentences of an article in a paragraph. The next paragraph contains the link "Read More...". Because the link is not in the same paragraph as the lead sentence, the user cannot easily discover what the link will let the user read more about.

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page: a paragraph reads '...for full pricing details, click here.' where the generic phrase 'click here' is the link but the purpose words ('full pricing details') precede it in the SAME sentence — the boundary near-PASS that is identical boilerplate to a failing page, rescued only by its enclosing sentence (G53).
pages.mechanism: The link's same-sentence programmatically determined context names the destination's purpose ('full pricing details') BEFORE the generic phrase, so a screen-reader user reading the paragraph hears the purpose first and can identify the link without leaving it; 2.4.4 is satisfied by link text combined with programmatic context per technique G53.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is a false-positive trap: phrase-blocklist heuristics flag the literal string 'click here' (accessible name confirmed as 'click here' via the AX tree) and report a violation, which is WRONG because the enclosing sentence rescues it under G53. No tool can parse the sentence, locate the purpose words, confirm they precede the link, and judge they describe the destination — that is the human in-context judgment.

citation.quote: A web page contains the sentence "To advertise on this page, click here." ... Although the link phrase 'click here' is not sufficient to understand the link, the information needed precedes the link in the same sentence.

pages.scenario: Restaurant site footer 'More' column: three list items, each containing only a link named 'Details', going to three different pages (menu, private events, gift cards). No text inside any <li> distinguishes them.
pages.mechanism: Each link's programmatically determined context is its own <li>, whose entire content is the word 'Details' — no same-list-item text, no aria-label/labelledby/describedby — so a screen-reader user hears 'Details, Details, Details' on the Links List and cannot tell which leads where; the visual 'More' heading is in a sibling element and is not programmatic link context.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three links have the non-empty accessible name 'Details' (confirmed via AX tree), so c487ae and axe link-name pass. A 'same text, different href' heuristic may warn but is neither necessary nor sufficient for 2.4.4 — WCAG explicitly permits repeated link text when context disambiguates (the PDF/mp3 book-list example). Whether each link's OWN list item supplies purpose requires a human reading the in-context text.

citation.quote: "Programmatically determined link context" is limited to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.

pages.scenario: Investor-relations 'Quarterly Disclosures' page: a link whose entire accessible name is the bare raw URL 'https://example.com/products/2024/q3-report.pdf', surrounded only by the words 'Document available at:' which name nothing.
pages.mechanism: The accessible name is the raw URL itself (confirmed via AX tree); a screen reader spells it out or reads it as an opaque token, and the user must mentally parse path segments to guess 'q3-report' is a Q3 report with no certainty of year/entity/type. The containing block adds only 'Document available at:', which names nothing — and WCAG G91/G53/H30 state the URI is 'generally not sufficiently descriptive'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The accessible name is a long, non-empty, UNIQUE string, so c487ae and axe link-name pass and duplicate-text heuristics never fire. A tool would have to recognize the name is a URL, parse its path, and judge whether the segments adequately convey purpose to a human — which WCAG frames as 'generally' insufficient, i.e. a case-by-case human judgment, and which no static check performs reliably.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe the purpose of a link in the text of the link. ... The URI of the destination is generally not sufficiently descriptive.

pages.scenario: Electronics shop: the SAME '>>' (raquo) chevron glyph link appears twice. In 'Editor's pick' it sits in the same sentence as a named product ('iPhone 15 Pro >>') and also carries an aria-label — that link PASSES. In 'Also trending' the identical glyph sits alone in its own paragraph with no product name in the block — that link FAILS. One page, opposite verdicts decided only by context.
pages.mechanism: The PASS link's accessible name is 'iPhone 15 Pro details' (aria-label) and is reinforced by the same-sentence product name (G53). The FAIL link's accessible name computes to the bare glyph '»' (confirmed via AX tree — non-empty), and its programmatic context (its own paragraph) contains no product name, heading, or ARIA association, so a user cannot determine it leads to the Aurora Bluetooth speaker. Identical glyph, opposite outcomes, decided purely by surrounding meaning.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty accessible names ('iPhone 15 Pro details' and the glyph '»'), so c487ae and axe link-name pass for both — critically the failing link is NOT an empty-name linter hit. A glyph like '>>'/'»' is not on phrase blocklists, so heuristic ambiguous-text checkers flag neither. Separating the rescued glyph from the orphaned one requires reading each enclosing sentence for a product name — a pure human meaning judgment.

citation.quote: The sentence enclosing the link provides context for an otherwise unclear link. The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.

pages.scenario: Public-health dashboard: a bar chart of childhood MMR coverage with a <figcaption> ending in a 'learn more' link. The caption sentence names the destination subject ('the methodology and clinic-level breakdown behind this 2025 dip in MMR coverage') immediately before the generic phrase, and the link lives INSIDE the figcaption — the hardest borderline PASS.
pages.mechanism: The link is a descendant of the <figcaption>, which is the link's containing block (and the figure's accessible name via aria-labelledby); the caption sentence names the subject BEFORE 'learn more', so a screen-reader user reading the caption hears the purpose first and can identify the link in context (2.4.4 same-block rule + G53). Accessible name confirmed as 'learn more' via AX tree.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: False-positive trap: 'learn more' is on phrase blocklists so heuristic tools flag a violation — incorrectly, because the figcaption rescues it. A name-presence tool passes it but for the wrong reason (it never reads context). Reaching the correct PASS requires a human to read the caption, locate the subject words ('2025 dip in MMR coverage'), confirm they sit in the link's containing block and precede the link, and judge they convey purpose; the chart data is an aria-label on role=img, opaque to text analysis.

citation.quote: This can be achieved by putting the description of the link in the same sentence, paragraph, list item, or table cell as the link, or in the table header cell for a link in a data table, because these are directly associated with the link itself.

pages.mechanism: Each <a> is in the a11y tree with role=link and a non-empty accessible name from aria-label (inner SVG is aria-hidden). The name is an asset filename / sprite id / placeholder, not the link's purpose, so the purpose cannot be determined from the link text and there is no programmatic context. Name-presence floor met; descriptive limb of 2.4.4 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only test that an interactive element has a non-empty accessible name; "img_2031", "settings.svg", "link" are all non-empty and distinct (verified: axe link-name = 7 passes, 0 violations). No tool renders the inline SVG to recognise a magnifying glass/gear/envelope or judge that a filename fails to convey search/settings/mail. The glyph-vs-name comparison is irreducibly visual and human-only.

citation.quote: When an image is the only content of a link, the text alternative for the image describes the unique function of the link.

pages.scenario: Local-news article breadcrumb: an icon link back to the Transit section index renders a LEFT-pointing chevron-plus-shaft (the universal back/previous glyph) via a data-URI SVG, destination /transit/index (where the reader came from). Its img alt is the non-empty word "forward" (copied from a paginator's next-arrow sprite); the visible "Transit desk" caption is aria-hidden, so the link's whole accessible name contradicts the glyph and the destination.
pages.mechanism: The <a> is exposed as role=link with accessible name "forward" (only the img alt contributes; the SVG is via src and the caption span is removed by aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP). A screen-reader user hears "forward" and expects to advance, but the link moves them backward to the index. Present, programmatically-determined name that misdescribes both the arrow's direction and the link purpose: F89's present-but-wrong sibling.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The link has a non-empty accessible name ("forward"), so axe passes it (verified: 2 passes, 0 violations). No checker decodes the data-URI SVG polyline to see the chevron points left, nor correlates that with a destination that is the page's previous location. Recognising "forward" is the opposite of a back-arrow's meaning needs a human to view the rendered icon and reason about direction and destination.

citation.quote: The text of, or associated with, the link is intended to describe the purpose of the link.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit food-bank donation footer with a social row of four icon-only brand links (Facebook, X/Twitter, Instagram, YouTube) pointing to four different platform profiles, but every link carries the identical non-empty aria-label "social media" (a themed CMS social-block applied one global label to every network).
pages.mechanism: All four <a> are role=link with the same accessible name "social media" (each SVG is aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP: four identical names). A screen-reader user listing links hears "social media" four times; the platform each opens lives only in the visual logo, absent from name and programmatic context. Each passes the non-empty floor but cannot have its purpose determined; 2.4.4 fails for the set.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each link has a non-empty accessible name, so axe passes the link-name rule (verified: 4 passes, 0 violations). A same-name heuristic cannot fire as a failure because, per fd3a94, identical-named links are only wrong when they serve different purposes — and a tool cannot know facebook.com/x.com/instagram.com/youtube.com are distinct destinations, nor read the rendered logos. Telling the brand glyphs apart and judging "social media" describes none specifically requires seeing each logo.

citation.quote: It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.

pages.scenario: Developer console API-keys data table with per-row pencil (edit) and trash (revoke) icon links. The custom icon set assigned each glyph a Unicode Private Use Area codepoint and auto-emitted the literal PUA character as the aria-label, so each link's accessible name is a single private-use character (U+E801 for edit, U+E803 for delete) — non-empty but semantically meaningless.
pages.mechanism: Each <a> is role=link with a non-empty accessible name of one PUA character (SVG is aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP: name.value codepoints are U+E801/U+E803). PUA codepoints carry no assigned Unicode meaning, so AT announces nothing useful (silence / "private use area E801" / fallback symbol), yet the link IS named. The trash action is destructive (revoke a key) with no spoken warning. Floor met; purpose undeterminable; 2.4.4 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The accname computation returns a non-empty string (one PUA character) for each link, so axe reports discernible text — VERIFIED: axe link-name = 6 passes, 0 violations even though Chrome's AX display shows name="" because the PUA glyph has no printable form. No tool resolves the PUA codepoint back to the pencil/trash glyph it was minted for, renders it, and judges the name fails to convey edit/revoke; that mapping lives only in the private font and the rendering.

citation.quote: This failure condition occurs when a link contains only non-text content, such as an image, and that link cannot be identified by an accessible name.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic recipe site (lang=ar dir=rtl). In a chicken-kabsa recipe card header, an icon-only link renders a download glyph (downward arrow into a tray) pointing to kabsa.pdf — purpose: save the recipe as PDF. But the CMS template bound the aria-label to the article-title variable, so the link is named "كبسة الدجاج بالخطوات" (the recipe's own name), well-formed meaningful Arabic that describes the article rather than the download action.
pages.mechanism: The <a> is role=link with accessible name "كبسة الدجاج بالخطوات" (confirmed via CDP). A screen-reader user hears the recipe title spoken twice (once as h1, once as this link) with no indication the second is a download control; they cannot tell it saves a PDF. Name present, programmatically determined, linguistically valid, but does not convey the link's purpose (the download action); 2.4.4 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The accessible name is a non-empty, correctly-scripted Arabic string with proper lang/dir, so axe passes the discernible-text rule (verified: 3 passes, 0 violations) and no language/empty-name finding fires. No tool renders the SVG to recognise a download glyph, reads that the href is a .pdf, or knows that naming a control after the surrounding article (not its action) misdescribes its purpose — requiring reading Arabic plus visual+semantic judgment.

citation.quote: In cases where the link takes one to a document or a web application, the name of the document or web application would be sufficient to describe the purpose of the link (which is to take you to the document or web application).

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS control: a municipal transit (Route 12 schedule) utility bar of three icon-only links — house (aria-label="Metro Transit home"), printer (aria-label="Print this schedule"), telephone (aria-label="Call rider services: 311", a tel: link). Each has a non-empty name AND the name correctly describes the rendered glyph and the link's purpose, so the page satisfies 2.4.4.
pages.mechanism: Each <a> is role=link with a non-empty accessible name from aria-label that matches its glyph and destination (confirmed via CDP: "Metro Transit home" / "Print this schedule" / "Call rider services: 311"; SVGs aria-hidden). A screen-reader user can determine each link's purpose from the link text alone. Both the name-presence floor (c487ae/F89) and the descriptive limb of 2.4.4 are met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is a true PASS, so there is no failure to miss — its role is to show the discriminator is glyph-vs-name AGREEMENT, not name presence. Crucially, the SAME automated signal ("has a non-empty name") is reported identically here and on failing cases 01-05 (verified: axe link-name = 3 passes, 0 violations, indistinguishable from the FAILs), which is exactly why tools cannot separate this PASS from those FAILs — only a human comparing each rendered glyph to its name can.

pages.scenario:
Bakery ordering page: one lead sentence (one

) contains two inline links both named 'order form', one targeting #cake-form (a bespoke priced celebration-cake quote) and one targeting #bread-form (a recurring Saturday bread subscription). Identical accessible name, identical same-DOM-node context, genuinely different on-page purposes resolvable via fragment anchors.
pages.mechanism: Two <a> in the same paragraph have identical accessible name 'order form' and therefore identical programmatically determined link context, but resolve to two #fragment sections that serve non-equivalent purposes (one-off priced cake quote vs recurring bread subscription). The disambiguating words ('for celebration cakes' / 'for sourdough and bread boxes') trail each link and are not part of, nor programmatically associated with, it — so a screen-reader links list yields 'order form / order form' with no way to choose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty identical accessible names and valid in-page hrefs, so link-name/discernible-text rules pass. The two links share the SAME DOM node as context, so any tool comparing 'programmatically determined context' sees them as identical and cannot tell the identity is the problem rather than evidence of equivalence. Deciding whether #cake-form and #bread-form serve equivalent or genuinely different purposes requires reading both sections and judging their meaning — an irreducible semantic judgment.

citation.quote: It is a best practice for links with the same destination to have consistent text (and this is a requirement per Success Criterion 3.2.4 Consistent Identification for pages in a set). It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.

pages.scenario:
Charity grant-spending page: one sentence (one

) offers the SAME four-row dataset in three takeaway formats, each behind an identical link named 'Download this data' — a PDF, an XLSX and a CSV delivered via self-contained data: URIs. Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, but the destinations are equivalent (same data, different format). PASS boundary control where the discriminator is purpose-equivalence.
pages.mechanism: Three <a download> with identical accessible name 'Download this data' in one paragraph resolve to three encodings (PDF/XLSX/CSV) of one identical dataset (the CSV data: URI literally encodes the same Food/Fuel/Children/Rent figures shown in the table). Per fd3a94's expectation, links sharing name+context PASS when they resolve to equivalent resources; 'same data, different file format' is the canonical equivalence (mirrored by the Understanding's HTML/PDF/mp3 'list of book titles' example). Every user gets the same content from any link, so each link's purpose — obtain this dataset — is determinable.
pages.primarySelector: p > a[download$=".pdf"], p > a[download$=".xlsx"], p > a[download$=".csv"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive duplicate-link heuristic would FALSELY flag three same-named links as a likely ambiguity failure; the tool cannot open the PDF/XLSX/CSV, parse them, and discover identical content. Conversely no name/role/href defect exists, so strict linters say nothing. Either way pass/fail hinges on the human-only judgment 'are these destinations the same data?' — exactly the equivalence call fd3a94 marks not fully automatable.

citation.quote: For each pair of links in each target set, one of the following is true: both links resolve to the same resource; or both links resolve to equivalent resources; or there is no visual information within the web page to let users know that both links resolve to non-equivalent resources.

pages.scenario:
Developer-tools SaaS contact card: one sentence (one

) has two inline links both named 'Email us', the first opening mailto:sales@latchkey.dev (pricing/seats/trial), the second mailto:support@latchkey.dev (production incidents/on-call). Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, non-equivalent mailto destinations routed to different teams; picking the wrong one sends an outage to the sales queue.
pages.mechanism: Two <a> in one paragraph have identical accessible name 'Email us' (hence identical programmatic context) but resolve to two different mailto recipients (sales@ vs support@) serving different functions. Per fd3a94's assumptions the mailto target (a URL) is not counted as disambiguating context, and the distinguishing clauses ('to talk pricing' / 'if something is broken') trail each link without being associated with it — so a links-list view gives 'Email us / Email us' and the user cannot pick the right inbox.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty identical names and valid mailto: hrefs, so link-name rules pass; sharing the same DOM-node context, a context comparison sees no difference. A tool would have to know that sales@ and support@ are different PURPOSES (not two aliases for one inbox) and that the surrounding prose makes the distinction available only to sighted readers — an organisational/semantic judgment beyond static analysis.

citation.quote: This rule assumes that reading the URL, such as from the status bar when the link is focused, is not considered part of the context, and therefore, it does not disambiguate links.

pages.scenario: Plant-care app pricing table laid out as a CSS Grid: two plans (Sprout $9/mo, Greenhouse $99/mo) side by side, each column ending in an identical 'Buy now' link. Each link sits in its own bare grid cell with NO plan name or price; the $9 / $99 price blocks are in separate grid cells positioned visually above their buttons. Disambiguation is conveyed purely by visual column alignment (verified: buy x-centers 123/549 align under price columns 237/663).
pages.mechanism: Two <a> named 'Buy now' resolve to non-equivalent destinations (#checkout-sprout $9 vs #checkout-greenhouse $99), but each link's programmatically determined link context (its own .buyrow cell) is equally bare — neither cell carries the plan or price, which lives in a sibling .price grid cell (the F63 'context not in the link's sentence/paragraph/cell' trap). Sighted users disambiguate by visual alignment under the price column; AT users get two identical 'Buy now' contexts. Because the page DOES convey the difference visually but not programmatically, fd3a94's 'no visual information' exemption does not apply and it fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have valid hrefs and identical non-empty names, so link-name passes; the price and plan exist in the DOM so no 'missing text' rule fires. A tool cannot tell the price is VISUALLY but not PROGRAMMATICALLY associated with each button (the association is grid geometry). Recognising that link-to-price-block alignment is the ONLY disambiguator requires rendering the layout and reasoning about spatial relationships, which the accessibility tree and static analysis do not capture.

pages.scenario:
Spanish-language (lang=es) public health-centre contact page (i18n long-tail): one sentence (one

) has two inline tel: links both named 'Llámanos' ('Call us'), each built from an aria-hidden SVG phone glyph plus text. The first dials tel:+34954112233 (the centre's routine appointments line), the second dials tel:112 (the pan-European emergency number). Identical accessible name (verified via Chromium AX snapshot), identical context, categorically different purposes.
pages.mechanism: Two <a> in one paragraph compute the identical accessible name 'Llámanos' because the phone glyph is aria-hidden, so context is identical, but the tel: targets are non-equivalent: a routine appointments switchboard vs the 112 emergency line (opposite urgency, opposite consequence). The disambiguating Spanish clauses ('para pedir una cita' vs 'si se trata de una urgencia vital') trail each link and are not associated with it, and the dialled number is not disambiguating context — so a links-list view yields 'Llámanos / Llámanos' and the user cannot tell the routine line from 112.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The glyph is correctly aria-hidden so each link has a clean non-empty identical accessible name (link-name passes); both tel: hrefs are valid and share the same DOM-node context. A tool would need to read Spanish prose to learn one link is for appointments and one for emergencies, AND know that tel:112 is the emergency number whose purpose differs categorically from a switchboard — locale-specific semantic reasoning beyond any static check.

citation.quote: This describes a failure condition when the context needed for understanding the purpose of a link is located in content that is not programmatically determined link context.

pages.scenario: Volunteer-run tech conference page (negative control): one paragraph contains two inline links both named 'contact us' in the same sentence-pair, one framed around accessibility needs and one around invoices/VAT receipts. Both point to the SAME #contact section — one shared organiser inbox handling every request (verified: 2 occurrences, 1 unique destination). Looks like the failing duplicate-name pattern but is benign because the destination is one and the same.
pages.mechanism: Two <a href="#contact"> with identical accessible name 'contact us' and identical context both resolve to the SAME in-page target (one <h2 id="contact"> shared-inbox section). Per fd3a94 this PASSES because 'both links resolve to the same resource' — the strongest equivalence. The surrounding clauses describe two topics (access vs finance) but both are served by one team at one address, so whichever link the user picks, the purpose (reach the organisers) is satisfied identically and no user is misled.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A duplicate-link heuristic would see two identical 'contact us' links and might FALSELY flag them as a candidate ambiguity failure; here the shared destination makes them benign. A static check cannot determine that #contact is a single shared inbox serving both stated topics rather than a page that ought to route access vs finance to different teams. Concluding 'same resource, therefore equivalent, therefore pass' requires reading the target section and judging its purpose — the same human equivalence judgment that fails case-01/03/05.
